title: You hire judgment, not paperwork
summary: A professional is only as useful as the question you give them, the scope you pay for and the facts you hand over. This lesson sets out the four tools that turn an adviser into an asset: the engagement letter, the written instruction, privilege, and the habit of challenging advice.
body:
You do not hire a lawyer, an accountant or an engineer to produce paper. You hire them to put trained judgment on a specific risk, and they can only do that if you define the question, the scope and the facts.

Recall

Q. Last week we looked at anti-avoidance rules. In plain terms, what does a general anti-avoidance rule ask about a transaction?

A. Whether the arrangement, although it follows the words of the law, achieves a tax result the rules were never meant to allow. It looks past the form to the substance. The exact test differs by country, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. Name the four families of tax on the real estate tax map.

A. Transfer taxes on the purchase, value-added tax or goods and services tax on supplies, tax on gains when you sell, and recapture of depreciation you claimed earlier.

Q. What is an implied land price?

A. The most a buyer can pay for land once you take the achievable rent or sale value, subtract every other cost, and leave the developer's required return. It is the residual, worked backward from public information.

Why this matters

A developer who runs his own projects will spend a meaningful share of soft costs on advisers: lawyers, accountants, tax advisers, appraisers, surveyors, engineers and architects. Most developers treat that spending as a cost to be minimised. The better frame is that each adviser is a risk-control device. A good adviser, well instructed, catches the clause that would have cost you the land, the tax character that would have cost you a quarter of the profit, or the soil condition that would have cost you the foundation. A poorly instructed adviser charges the same fees and catches none of it. The difference is almost entirely in how you engage them.

The engagement letter: who, what, how much, and what is left out

Plain English first. An engagement letter is the contract between you and the professional. It answers four questions: who the client is, what work is included, how the fee works, and what is excluded.

The professional framing has two terms worth owning. The first is the engagement letter itself. The second is the scope of retainer, meaning the precise boundary of the work the professional has agreed to do. Courts and regulators in most common-law systems look closely at that boundary when something goes wrong, because a professional is usually responsible for what they were engaged to do, not for everything they might have noticed. Verify that against the primary source in the place where you are working before you rely on it.

Worked example. Two developers each ask a lawyer to look at a land purchase. Developer A writes: "Please review the attached agreement." Developer B writes: "Please review the attached agreement of purchase and sale. I intend to build roughly 60 rental units. Advise on: whether the conditions give me enough time for financing and soil testing; whether any registered easement or covenant on title limits that use; and what happens to my deposit if I terminate. I need your advice by the 14th because the condition date is the 21st." Both pay similar fees. Developer A gets a markup of typographical issues and a few general comments. Developer B gets advice aimed at the three things that can actually lose him money. Notice that B told the lawyer the intended use. Without that fact, no lawyer can tell you that a covenant on title is fatal to your plan.

The question of who the client is matters more than it looks. If a lawyer acts for a joint venture, the lawyer owes duties to the venture, not to you personally. If you and your partner later disagree, that lawyer may not be able to advise you at all. When your interests and the entity's interests could diverge, you need your own adviser as well.

The written instruction

Plain English: say exactly what you want answered, give every fact that matters, and put it in writing. A phone call is fine for discussion. The instruction itself should be written, because it becomes the record of what you asked and what the adviser knew when they answered.

A good instruction has five parts. The decision you have to make. The specific questions you need answered. The facts, including the unhelpful ones. The documents attached. The deadline and why it matters. That last part is not a courtesy. An adviser who knows that a condition expires in seven days will prioritise differently from one who thinks there is no rush.

The most expensive habit in professional services is withholding a fact because you hope it will not matter. An adviser cannot advise on what they were not told, and in most systems their advice is judged against the facts you gave them. If you hide the fact that the vendor already gave you a side letter, the advice you receive on the main agreement is worth very little.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: "An adviser answers the question I asked, on the facts I gave, within the scope I paid for. If any of those three is wrong, the advice is wrong."

Privilege, and why you protect it

Plain English: in many legal systems, communications between you and your lawyer for the purpose of legal advice are protected from disclosure. That protection is called privilege. It belongs to you, the client, not to the lawyer, and you can lose it by sharing the advice with people outside the relationship.

The professional framing: privilege generally does not cover the underlying facts, only the confidential advice, and it is usually much narrower for advisers who are not lawyers. In many places, a tax opinion from an accountant is not protected the way a tax opinion from a lawyer may be. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. We will go deeper on this on Day 4.

Worked example. A developer receives a frank memo from his lawyer saying a dispute with the contractor is weaker than he hoped. Proud of having good counsel, he forwards it to his lender and his equity partner. Later the dispute goes to arbitration. Depending on the rules that apply, he may have waived the protection over that memo, and the contractor may be able to see his own lawyer's assessment of his weaknesses. The fix was simple: tell the lender and the partner the conclusion and the next step, in his own words, and keep the memo inside the solicitor-client relationship.

How the best do it

Large owners and developers rarely let advisers drift. The common practice is a short panel of pre-approved firms on standing terms, a written budget for each matter, one named person inside the owner who instructs and receives advice, and a quarterly review of what each adviser delivered against what was paid. A small developer can copy all four: keep a one-page instruction template, name yourself as the only person who instructs, ask for a budget before work starts, and keep a running file of each adviser's calls that turned out right or wrong.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is not a bad adviser. It is a good adviser answering the wrong question. The control is the written instruction, read back. Before work starts, ask the adviser to restate in one paragraph what they understand they are being asked to do and what is out of scope. If their paragraph does not match yours, you have found the problem for the price of an email.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hires on fees and personality, sends a bundle of documents with the word "thoughts?", and then treats the reply as a guarantee. Three errors at once: no defined question, no defined scope, and no challenge. Advice is an input to your decision, not a substitute for it. You still own the decision.

Callback

In Week 20 we drew a hard line between documents that bind and documents that do not, and saw that a letter of intent can bind on some clauses and not others. The same discipline applies here. An engagement letter is a contract. Read its exclusions as carefully as you would read the exclusions in a construction contract, because the exclusion clause is where the adviser has quietly told you what they will not be responsible for.

Recap

Hire judgment, not paperwork. Define the client, the scope and the fee in an engagement letter. Instruct in writing with the decision, the questions, all the facts and the deadline. Protect privilege by sharing conclusions, not advice. Then challenge what comes back.

Next: Ford, with Cole assisting, on what happened when the auditors and lawyers became part of the problem at Enron.
checklist: Confirm in writing who the client is and whether you need your own separate adviser
Read the engagement letter's exclusions before you sign it
State the decision you have to make at the top of every instruction
List the specific questions, numbered
Give every material fact, including the unhelpful ones
Attach the documents and state the deadline and why it matters
Ask the adviser to restate the scope in one paragraph before work starts
Share conclusions with third parties, not the privileged advice itself
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, you do not hire professionals to produce paper. You hire them to put trained judgment on a specific risk. Four tools make that work. First, the engagement letter: it says who the client is, what is included, how the fee works and what is excluded, and the exclusions matter most. Second, the written instruction: the decision you face, the numbered questions, every fact including the bad ones, the documents and the deadline. An adviser answers the question you asked, on the facts you gave, within the scope you paid for. If any of those is wrong, the advice is wrong. Third, privilege: in many systems your confidential legal advice is protected, but you can lose that by forwarding it, so share conclusions, not memos. Fourth, challenge what comes back. Before any work starts, ask the adviser to restate the scope in one paragraph. If it does not match yours, you have found the problem for the price of an email.
terms: Engagement letter — the contract with a professional setting out who the client is, the work included, the fee and the exclusions.
Scope of retainer — the precise boundary of the work a professional has agreed to do, which usually defines what they are responsible for.
Privilege — in many legal systems, protection from disclosure for confidential lawyer-client communications made for legal advice; it belongs to the client and can be waived.

hostile.q: Your lawyer reviewed the purchase agreement and still missed the restrictive covenant that killed your plan. Why should I trust your process with my equity?
hostile.a: Because I changed the process, not just the lawyer. The review was instructed without the intended use, so the covenant looked harmless. Every instruction now states the decision, the intended use and numbered questions, and the adviser restates the scope in writing before work starts. I can show you the template and the last three instructions.

title: Enron: when the advisers became part of the structure
summary: Enron collapsed in 2001, and its auditor Arthur Andersen collapsed with it. This lesson takes the case through seven steps to show how scope, fees and dependence can turn professionals from a control into a component of the failure.
body:
Enron failed because of its own management, but it was able to fail as large and as late as it did because the professionals around it were scoped, paid and positioned in ways that blunted their independence. That is the lesson for anyone who hires advisers.

Recall

Q. In the last lesson, what were the four questions every engagement letter must answer?

A. Who the client is, what work is included, how the fee works, and what is excluded.

Q. On the real estate tax map, what is recapture?

A. Tax that claws back depreciation you claimed in earlier years when you sell an asset for more than its depreciated tax value.

Q. When you reverse engineer a deal, why do you start from the finished outcome?

A. Because the market tells you the end value, and working backward shows what every other number, including land, had to be for the deal to make sense.

Why this matters

You will rely on auditors, accountants, lawyers, appraisers and engineers who are paid by you. That creates a quiet tension: the person checking your work depends on you for income. Most of the time the profession's standards hold that tension in place. Enron is the clearest public case of what happens when they do not. Ford leads this lesson; Cole, our audit and integrity lead, assists on the professional and legal side.

The case in brief

Enron was a Houston energy company that grew into energy trading and other businesses through the 1990s. It used a large number of special purpose entities, separate companies that kept debt and losses off Enron's own balance sheet. Some were run by Enron's own chief financial officer, Andrew Fastow. Its auditor was Arthur Andersen, then one of the largest accounting firms in the world, which also earned consulting fees from Enron. In the second half of 2001 Enron announced large losses and restated earlier results. It filed for bankruptcy protection in December 2001. Andersen staff destroyed Enron-related documents, the firm was convicted of obstruction of justice in 2002, and although the United States Supreme Court overturned that conviction in 2005, the firm had already lost its clients and effectively ceased to operate as an auditor. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act followed in 2002. I am deliberately leaving out dollar figures I cannot verify here.

The seven steps

  1. Timeline. Rapid growth and new trading businesses in the 1990s; growing use of off-balance-sheet entities; an internal warning letter to the chairman in August 2001 from an Enron vice president, Sherron Watkins; restatement and collapse in the autumn of 2001; bankruptcy in December; the auditor's conviction in 2002.
  2. Key decisions. Management chose structures designed to keep debt off the reported balance sheet. Officers were allowed to run entities that dealt with the company. The auditor accepted those structures. When the internal warning arrived, an outside law firm was asked to review it, and public accounts of that review describe its scope as limited, with the accounting treatment largely not second-guessed.
  3. Assumptions. That rising stock prices would keep the structures solvent. That technical compliance with accounting rules was the same as fair presentation. That a review scoped not to question the accounting could still give comfort about the accounting.
  4. Incentives. Executives were rewarded for reported earnings and a high share price. The audit firm earned both audit and consulting fees from one very large client, which raised the cost to the firm of saying no. Officers running the related entities had personal economic interests on the other side of the table.
  5. Warning signs ignored. Earnings that did not turn into cash. Related-party transactions with the company's own officers. Complexity that even sophisticated analysts said they could not follow. A written warning from inside.
  6. Point of no return. By the time the warning letter was reviewed with a narrow scope in 2001, the structures depended on the share price holding up. Once confidence broke, there was no way back.
  7. Root cause. Gatekeepers whose independence had been eroded by fees, scope and closeness. The checking function existed on paper and did not work in practice.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: "A review that is told not to look at the problem is not a review of the problem."

What it means for a developer

You will never run a company like Enron, but the mechanism scales down perfectly. Worked example one, a composite. This is a composite example. A developer needs an appraisal to satisfy a lender's loan-to-value test. He tells the appraiser the number the deal "needs", sends only the comparable sales that support it, and says he will use the same appraiser on the next three projects. The appraisal arrives at exactly the number. Nothing illegal has necessarily happened, but the appraisal is now a mirror, not a check, and the lender, the investors and the developer himself are all relying on it.

Worked example two, also a composite. A developer asks his accountant to "confirm the project company's costs are capitalised correctly" and supplies only the costs he has already classified. The accountant confirms the arithmetic. Months later a tax reviewer reclassifies a block of costs, and the developer discovers the accountant was never asked whether the classification was right, only whether the totals added up. Scope did the damage.

Cole's point from the audit side: independence is not a personality trait. It is a set of conditions. The adviser's fee does not depend on the answer. The adviser has access to all the facts, not a curated set. The adviser is scoped to look where the risk is. And the adviser has a way to tell someone senior if they disagree.

What the system changed afterwards

After Enron and other failures of the same period, the United States passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in 2002. In broad terms it created a public oversight board for auditors of listed companies, restricted the non-audit services an auditor may sell to its own audit client, and put more responsibility on audit committees and on the executives who certify financial statements. The detail is beyond this lesson and applies to public companies in one country, so verify any specific requirement against the primary source before you rely on it. The design logic is what matters to you: separate the person who checks from the person who sells, give the checker a line to someone independent of management, and make the people who sign accountable for what they sign. You can build those three ideas into a private project company with a one-page policy and a standing agenda item at every partner meeting.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that you, without intending to, buy agreement instead of judgment, by scoping narrowly, curating the facts or signalling the answer you want. The control is to write the scope around the risk, not around the comfort you want, and to supply the full file, including the documents that hurt.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats a clean opinion as proof that the underlying position is sound. An opinion is only as good as its scope, its facts and its independence. Read the scope paragraph and the list of documents reviewed before you read the conclusion.

Callback

Back in Week 3 we studied incentives: people tend to do what they are paid to do. Enron is that principle applied to gatekeepers. An auditor earning large consulting fees from the same client, an officer earning from both sides of a related-party deal, and executives paid on reported earnings all behaved in line with their incentives. When you design an adviser relationship, design the incentive first.

Recap

Enron failed through management choices, but the professionals around it were scoped, paid and positioned in ways that weakened the check they were supposed to provide. For a developer, the risk is buying agreement instead of judgment. Rule 25: I scope every adviser to look where the risk is, give them the whole file, and never let their fee depend on agreeing with me.

Next: Nadia on the money side of advisers, what they cost and what they save.
checklist: Write each adviser's scope around the risk, not around the comfort you want
Give the adviser the full file, including the documents that hurt your position
Never tell an appraiser or valuer the number the deal needs
Check that no adviser's fee depends on the answer they give
Read the scope paragraph and documents-reviewed list before the conclusion
Treat related-party dealings as a warning sign to be reviewed independently
Act on internal warnings with a review scoped to test them, not to close them
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, Enron collapsed in 2001 and its auditor, Arthur Andersen, went down with it. Management built off-balance-sheet entities, some run by its own chief financial officer. The auditor accepted them while also earning consulting fees from the same client. When an internal warning arrived in August 2001, an outside review was scoped narrowly. Bankruptcy followed in December. The root cause was gatekeepers whose independence had been worn down by fees, scope and closeness. The lesson scales down to every project you run. If you tell an appraiser the number you need, curate the facts for your accountant, or scope a review so it cannot find the problem, you have bought agreement instead of judgment. Independence is a set of conditions: the fee does not depend on the answer, the adviser sees all the facts, and the scope points at the risk. Rule 25: I scope every adviser to look where the risk is, give them the whole file, and never let their fee depend on agreeing with me.
terms: Special purpose entity — a separate company set up for one narrow purpose, sometimes used to keep assets or debt off another company's balance sheet.
Gatekeeper — a professional, such as an auditor, lawyer or appraiser, whose sign-off others rely on as an independent check.
Related-party transaction — a deal between a company and someone connected to it, such as an officer, which needs independent review because interests conflict.

hostile.q: Your appraiser has valued your last four projects. How do I know this appraisal is independent and not just your number?
hostile.a: Fair question. The engagement letter states the appraiser's fee is fixed regardless of value, the appraiser received the full comparable set including the weak sales, and I gave no target. You are welcome to commission a review appraisal from a firm of your choice, and I will share the instruction letter I sent.

rule: Rule 25: I scope every adviser to look where the risk is, give them the whole file, and never let their fee depend on agreeing with me.

title: What advisers cost, and what they save
summary: Adviser fees are a soft cost that barely moves yield on cost, while the risks good advisers catch can move the whole return. This lesson shows how to budget professional fees, choose a fee structure and judge advice by the expected loss it prevents.
body:
Professional fees are usually a small line in the budget and a large line in the outcome. Budget them deliberately, choose the fee structure that matches the uncertainty, and judge each adviser by the expected loss they prevent, not by their hourly rate.

Recall

Q. When someone in a meeting pushes an aggressive tax position, what is the first question to ask?

A. What is the business purpose apart from the tax result? If there is none, you are looking at substance-over-form risk, and you need advice before you go further.

Q. How does a transfer tax on purchase affect your return?

A. It is paid up front, increases total project cost and the equity needed, and usually lowers yield on cost and internal rate of return unless the price adjusts to absorb it.

Q. In reverse engineering a deal, what does a higher required return do to the implied land price?

A. It lowers it. The buyer needs more of the end value as profit, so less is left for land.

Why this matters

Developers often cut adviser budgets first because the saving is visible and immediate, while the cost of missing something is invisible until it lands. For a developer and wealth builder, the right question is not how much the lawyer costs. It is how much risk each dollar of professional fees removes from the project and from your personal balance sheet.

Where fees sit in the budget

Plain English: lawyers, accountants, tax advisers, appraisers, surveyors and consultants are paid out of soft costs, the part of the budget that is not bricks and labour. Some fees are capitalised into the cost of the asset, meaning they are added to its cost rather than expensed immediately; others are expensed. How each fee is treated depends on accounting rules and tax law, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. A project costs $20,000,000 in total and is expected to produce stabilised net operating income (NOI) of $1,300,000 a year. Yield on cost is NOI divided by total cost: $1,300,000 divided by $20,000,000 equals 6.50 percent. Now suppose adviser fees run $150,000 over budget. Total cost becomes $20,150,000. Yield on cost becomes $1,300,000 divided by $20,150,000, which is 6.45 percent. The overrun cost you five hundredths of a percentage point.

Now suppose a missed easement forces you to drop four units, cutting stabilised NOI by $80,000 a year. NOI falls to $1,220,000 and yield on cost falls to 6.10 percent. At a hypothetical 5.50 percent capitalisation rate, $80,000 of lost NOI is $80,000 divided by 0.055, about $1,455,000 of lost value. That is nearly ten times the fee overrun. The asymmetry is the whole point.

Choosing a fee structure

There are four common structures. These are commercial practice, not standards, and what is permitted varies by profession and place. Hourly: you pay for time, so you carry the risk that the work takes longer. Fixed fee: the adviser carries that risk and prices it in. Capped fee: hourly up to a ceiling, a compromise. Contingent or success fee: payment depends on an outcome, which is permitted for some work in some places and restricted or forbidden for others, especially audit work, because it ties the fee to the answer.

Match the structure to the uncertainty. When the scope is clear and repeatable, such as a standard title search, a fixed fee is efficient. When the scope cannot be known in advance, such as a dispute, hourly with a budget and monthly reporting is usually more honest than a fixed fee padded for every contingency. Never use a fee that pays more for a particular answer on any question where you are relying on independent judgment. That is Rule 25 from yesterday.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A lawyer offers $15,000 fixed, or hourly at a blended $375 an hour with an estimate of 40 hours. The estimate is also $15,000. But experience says there is a 30 percent chance the negotiation drags and the hours run 50 percent over. Expected hourly cost is 70 percent times $15,000 plus 30 percent times $22,500. That is $10,500 plus $6,750, or $17,250. The fixed fee is worth $2,250 to you in expectation, as long as the scope in the engagement letter genuinely covers the drag.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: "Fees move yield on cost by basis points. Missed risks move it by percentage points."

Advice as expected loss avoided

The professional framing is expected value: probability of a loss multiplied by its size. Suppose a tax review costs $40,000. Without it, you estimate a 10 percent chance of a reassessment, meaning a tax authority revising your tax bill, of $800,000 including interest and penalties. The expected loss is $80,000. If the review reliably removes that risk, it is worth roughly twice its fee before you even count your time and stress. If the probability were 2 percent, the expected loss would be $16,000 and the same review would not pay for itself on these numbers alone. These probabilities are judgments, not facts, so write down how you arrived at them.

The cost of slow advice

There is a second cost that never appears on an invoice: time. While you wait for advice, carrying costs keep running. Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. You hold land with a $5,000,000 loan at 8 percent interest. Annual interest is $5,000,000 times 0.08, which is $400,000, or about $33,300 a month and roughly $1,100 a day. If a cheaper adviser takes three weeks longer to turn around the same purchase-agreement review, that delay costs about 21 days times $1,100, roughly $23,000, which may exceed the saving on the fee. Put the deadline and the reason for it in the instruction, ask for a turnaround date in writing, and include turnaround in the way you compare quotes. Speed without quality is worthless, but quality that arrives after the condition date is worth nothing either.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for the personal balance sheet. Professional fees for structuring, estate planning and tax advice protect assets you will hold for decades, so their payback period is long and real. Advisers also protect against contingent liabilities, meaning obligations that only become real if something happens, such as a personal guarantee being called. A contingent liability does not appear on most people's personal net worth statement, and that is exactly why it is dangerous. Ask your advisers to list every contingent liability you carry. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal planning.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an uncontrolled hourly burn on a matter nobody is watching, followed by a panic decision to stop the advice halfway, which buys the cost without the protection. The control is a written budget for every matter, monthly invoices with time entries, and a forecast of cost to complete that you review against the risk the advice is meant to remove.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner picks the cheapest quote for the most important advice. On a site with a known title problem, the difference between a cheap and a strong lawyer might be a few thousand dollars. The difference between their outcomes can be the project.

Callback

In Week 13 we separated hard, soft, finance and land costs and gave contingency its own line. Professional fees belong in soft costs with their own budget lines by discipline, and a modest professional-fee contingency belongs beside them, because disputes and redesigns are exactly the events that drive unplanned advice.

Recap

Adviser fees barely move yield on cost; the risks advisers catch can move it materially. Budget fees by discipline, choose the fee structure that fits the uncertainty, never pay for a particular answer, and judge advice by expected loss avoided.

Next: LEX on the rules that govern professionals, including privilege, conflicts and duty of care.
checklist: Give every adviser discipline its own soft-cost budget line
Add a modest professional-fee contingency beside those lines
Match the fee structure to how uncertain the scope is
Refuse any fee that pays more for a particular answer
Ask for monthly invoices with time entries and a cost-to-complete forecast
Estimate the expected loss each piece of advice is meant to prevent, and write down how
Ask advisers to list every contingent liability you personally carry
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, professional fees are a small line in the budget and a large line in the outcome. On a hypothetical $20 million project with $1.3 million of net operating income, a $150,000 fee overrun moves yield on cost from 6.50 to 6.45 percent. A missed easement that costs four units and $80,000 of income moves it to 6.10 percent and, at a 5.5 percent cap rate, wipes out about $1.45 million of value. Fees move returns by basis points; missed risks move them by percentage points. So budget fees by discipline, choose hourly, fixed or capped fees to match how uncertain the work is, and never pay a fee that rises with a particular answer. Judge advice as expected loss avoided: probability times size. A $40,000 review that removes a 10 percent chance of an $800,000 reassessment is worth about twice its cost. And on your personal balance sheet, ask your advisers to list every contingent liability you carry.
terms: Soft costs — project costs other than land, construction and finance, including design, legal, accounting and other professional fees.
Expected loss — the probability of a loss multiplied by its size, used to judge whether a control is worth its cost.
Contingent liability — an obligation that becomes real only if a future event happens, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: Your soft costs include $400,000 of professional fees on a modest project. Why is that not just fat I should cut?
hostile.a: Because each line is tied to a named risk with a budget and a monthly report. The title and land-use work alone protects income that, at our cap rate, carries well over a million dollars of value. I can walk you through each line, what it protects and the expected loss it removes, and I will cut any line where that case does not hold.

title: Privilege, conflicts and the duty an adviser owes you
summary: The rules around professionals decide what stays confidential, whose side the adviser is on and what you can recover when advice is wrong. This lesson covers privilege and how it is lost, conflicts of interest, and professional liability, with a conceptual comparison of Canada and Guyana.
body:
Three rules govern your relationship with a professional: what stays confidential, whose interests they must serve, and what happens when they get it wrong. Know the shape of each before you need it, because you usually need it in a dispute, when it is too late to learn.

Recall

Q. What separates tax avoidance from tax evasion?

A. Avoidance uses the law to reduce tax, and may still be challenged under anti-avoidance rules. Evasion is concealment or misrepresentation of facts to escape tax that is legally owed, and it is an offence.

Q. Who usually has to charge and remit a value-added tax or goods and services tax on a real estate sale?

A. It depends on the rules of the place and the type of property, and sometimes the obligation shifts to the buyer. That is exactly why you verify it against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. Name two public sources you can use to reverse engineer a competitor's deal.

A. The land registry, which shows price and charges, and building permit or planning records, which show scope and sometimes construction value.

Why this matters

As an owner you will instruct advisers on land purchases, financing, disputes and tax. If you lose privilege, your lawyer's frank assessment can end up in your opponent's hands. If your adviser has a conflict, their advice may tilt toward someone else. If their advice is negligent and you signed an engagement letter capping their liability at their fee, your recovery may be a fraction of your loss. None of these are rare.

Privilege and how it is lost

Plain English: in common-law systems, confidential communications between you and your lawyer, made to get or give legal advice, are generally protected from disclosure. This is usually called legal advice privilege or solicitor-client privilege. A second kind, litigation privilege, generally protects material prepared for the main purpose of actual or reasonably expected litigation, and can extend to reports from third parties such as engineers if they were commissioned for that purpose. The tests differ by jurisdiction, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The professional framing has three points. First, privilege belongs to the client, so only you can give it up. Second, it usually protects advice, not facts. The soil report showing contamination is a fact; your lawyer's view on who pays for it is advice. Third, it can be lost by waiver, meaning disclosure outside the protected relationship, whether deliberate or careless.

Worked example one. A building envelope is leaking. The developer's lawyer, expecting a claim against the contractor, retains an engineer to investigate and report to the lawyer. Separately, the developer's property manager commissions a second engineer to fix the leak. The first report, prepared for anticipated litigation and routed through counsel, has a reasonable argument for protection. The second, prepared for operations, very likely does not. If the developer emails the first report to the contractor in frustration, he may have waived protection over it. The control: route anticipated-dispute investigations through counsel, label them, keep a distribution list, and send the other side your position, not your evidence.

Two practical warnings. Advice from accountants and tax advisers who are not lawyers is, in many places, not protected the way legal advice is. And sharing advice with a lender, partner or insurer may or may not be protected by a common-interest arrangement depending on the facts and the place. Ask counsel before you share, not after.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: "Privilege is mine, it covers advice and not facts, and I lose it the moment I share it carelessly."

Conflicts of interest

Plain English: a professional owes you loyalty. If they act for someone whose interests run against yours in the same matter, or are influenced by their own interest, their advice is compromised. Professional rules generally require them to identify conflicts, disclose them and, in many cases, decline to act or obtain informed consent.

Worked example two. A landowner and a developer agree to form a joint venture. To save money, they ask one lawyer to "paper the deal for both of us". On the day the parties disagree about the value of the land contributed, that lawyer cannot take either side, and both lose the person who knows the file best. The control: separate counsel for each party on anything where your interests can diverge, which in a joint venture means almost everything. The same applies to a real estate agent paid by the vendor and an appraiser chosen by the borrower. Ask every adviser, in writing, whether they act or have acted for anyone else on the deal.

Duty of care and limiting it

Plain English: a professional who gives advice owes a duty to take reasonable care, judged against what a reasonably competent member of that profession would do. If they fall short and you suffer loss caused by it, you may have a claim in negligence, contract or both.

The professional framing: engagement letters often limit that liability, for example by capping it at a multiple of fees, excluding indirect losses, or limiting claims to the firm rather than individuals. Some professions face rules restricting how far they may limit liability; others may limit it freely. A limitation period, the deadline for bringing a claim, also applies and varies widely. Verify each of these against the primary source and the current professional rules before you rely on them. Read the limitation clause in every engagement letter and ask whether the cap is sensible against the size of the risk the adviser is handling. A cap equal to a $20,000 fee on advice protecting a $5,000,000 land position deserves a conversation, and confirmation that the firm carries professional liability insurance.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison only; verify every point against the primary source. Both countries inherited the common-law tradition, so privilege, duty of care and fiduciary loyalty are recognisable in both. In Canada, the legal profession is regulated province by province through law societies, and the country's highest courts have treated solicitor-client privilege as a fundamental protection. Guyana is a single jurisdiction where lawyers practise as attorneys-at-law under national legislation, and its final appellate court is the Caribbean Court of Justice rather than a domestic supreme court of last resort. Parts of Guyanese land and conveyancing practice carry historical influences from its Roman-Dutch past, so the documents and procedures your lawyer handles may differ from the Canadian equivalents even where the principles feel familiar. The practical lesson: use advisers qualified in the jurisdiction where the asset, the entity and the dispute sit, and do not assume a rule carries across a border because the vocabulary does.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer qualified in the relevant jurisdiction.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is losing privilege through casual forwarding during a dispute, when emotions run high and the temptation to prove you are right is strongest. The control is a standing rule: during any dispute, no legal advice leaves your inbox without counsel's agreement, and you send the other side positions, not memos.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner shares one lawyer with a partner to save fees and signs engagement letters without reading the liability cap. Both feel efficient until the first disagreement or the first mistake.

Callback

In Week 21 we covered agency: an agent acting within their authority can bind their principal. Professionals often act as your agent, negotiating and signing on your behalf. Give them written authority with limits, because what they agree within that authority may bind you, and what they agree outside it creates a fight you do not need.

Recap

Privilege is yours, covers advice not facts, and is lost by careless sharing. Conflicts require separate advisers whenever interests can diverge. Duty of care can be limited in the engagement letter, so read the cap and check the insurance. Across borders, the vocabulary travels further than the rules.

Next: Vera on auditing a professional's invoice line by line.
checklist: Route investigations for an expected dispute through counsel and label them
Keep a distribution list for every piece of legal advice
Send the other side positions, never your lawyer's memos
Ask counsel before sharing advice with a lender, partner or insurer
Ask every adviser in writing whether they act for anyone else on the deal
Use separate counsel wherever your interests and a partner's can diverge
Read the liability cap and confirm professional liability insurance
Use advisers qualified where the asset, the entity and the dispute sit
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, three rules govern your relationship with a professional. First, privilege. In common-law systems, confidential legal advice is generally protected, and material prepared mainly for expected litigation can be too. It belongs to you, it covers advice and not facts, and you lose it by careless sharing. During a dispute, send positions, never memos. Second, conflicts. A professional owes you loyalty, so whenever your interests and a partner's can diverge, each of you needs your own lawyer. Third, duty of care. Advisers must take reasonable care, but engagement letters often cap their liability, sometimes at the fee. Read the cap and confirm the insurance against the size of the risk. Canada and Guyana share the common-law tradition, but Canada regulates lawyers province by province while Guyana is one jurisdiction with the Caribbean Court of Justice as its final court. Verify against the primary source, and use advisers qualified where the asset sits.
terms: Litigation privilege — protection, in many common-law systems, for material prepared mainly for actual or reasonably expected litigation.
Waiver — giving up a protection such as privilege, often by sharing protected material outside the protected relationship.
Limitation of liability — a contract clause capping or excluding what a party must pay if it is at fault, often expressed as a multiple of fees.

hostile.q: You want my investment in a joint venture where your lawyer drafted the agreement. Who protects me?
hostile.a: You do, through your own counsel, and I will insist on it. Our interests can diverge on valuation, capital calls and exits, so one lawyer cannot serve both of us. My counsel drafts; yours reviews and negotiates. I will also confirm in writing that my lawyer has not advised you on anything.

title: Auditing a professional's invoice, line by line
summary: A professional's invoice is a record you can test against the engagement letter. This lesson works through a hypothetical legal invoice to find rate errors, duplicates, out-of-scope work and vague entries, then forecasts the cost at completion against the fee cap.
body:
An invoice is evidence of work done, and like any evidence it can be tested. Compare every line to the engagement letter, separate what is payable from what is queried, and forecast where the matter will finish before it finishes.

Recall

Q. On Day 1 this week, what five parts make a good written instruction?

A. The decision you must make, numbered questions, all material facts including the bad ones, the documents, and the deadline with its reason.

Q. When you calculate the effect of a transfer tax on equity, where does the tax go in sources and uses?

A. In uses, as an acquisition cost. It increases the total funding needed, and unless debt covers it, equity rises by the same amount.

Q. When reverse engineering a competitor's land price, what is the first number you need?

A. A credible end value, from rents and a capitalisation rate or from comparable sales, because everything else is subtracted from it.

Why this matters

Over a development career you will pay many invoices from lawyers, consultants and contractors. Most are honest. Many still contain errors, because time recording is done in a hurry by busy people. A disciplined review recovers money, but its bigger value is early warning: an invoice that is running hot at 60 percent complete tells you the matter will blow its budget long before the final bill arrives.

The engagement and the invoice

All figures are hypothetical. The engagement letter says: review and negotiate a purchase agreement for a development site; zoning advice is excluded; estimated 40 hours; fees capped at $18,000 excluding disbursements and any applicable sales tax; rates are partner $500 an hour, associate $300 an hour and law clerk $150 an hour; disbursements, meaning out-of-pocket costs like search fees and couriers, are charged at cost.

The first invoice arrives. The lawyer reports the work is 60 percent complete.

LineWhoHoursRate billedAmount
Review, negotiation and calls, all entriesPartner12.0$500$6,000
Drafting and review, all entriesAssociate30.0$325$9,750
Title searches and document managementClerk10.0$150$1,500
Fees subtotal52.0$17,250
Search fees and courier$400
Administrative charge at 10 percent of disbursements$40

The detailed time entries show three things worth noting. One partner entry of 1.5 hours for a call with the vendor's lawyer appears twice on the same date with the same description. One associate entry reads "Attention to file, 6.5 hours" with no detail. One associate entry reads "Research zoning permissions, 4.0 hours".

Step by step: the line review

Step 1, rates. The letter says associate time is $300 an hour; the invoice bills $325. Overbilling is 30.0 hours times $25 an hour, which is $750.

Step 2, duplicates. The 1.5-hour partner call appears twice. Remove one: 1.5 hours times $500 an hour is $750.

Step 3, scope. Zoning advice is excluded in the letter. The 4.0 hours of zoning research is out of scope: 4.0 hours times $300 an hour is $1,200. This may have been useful work, but it needs a written change in scope that you approved. Do not pay it as part of this engagement until that happens.

Step 4, vague entries. "Attention to file, 6.5 hours" is what reviewers call block billing: a large block of time with no description of the tasks. You cannot test it, so you query it rather than reject it. 6.5 hours times $300 an hour is $1,950 held pending a breakdown.

Step 5, disbursements. The letter says at cost, so the $40 administrative charge is not payable.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: "Rate, duplicate, scope, vague entry, disbursements. Five checks, every invoice."

The result

Accepted fees are the $17,250 subtotal minus the $750 rate error, minus the $750 duplicate, minus the $1,200 out-of-scope work. That is $14,550. Of that, $1,950 is held pending the breakdown, so the amount payable now is $14,550 minus $1,950, or $12,600 of fees, plus $400 of disbursements at cost. Sales tax on professional fees may apply on top, depending on where you are, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Your record: write a short dispute note listing each item, the clause in the engagement letter it relies on, and the amount. Send it the same week, and keep it with the invoice. That note is your evidence if the matter is ever reviewed.

Vera's records rule: keep three things together in one folder for each adviser. The signed engagement letter and every written scope change. Every invoice with its time entries, not just the summary page. And every dispute note with the reply. If a lender's monitor, an investor or an auditor later asks why professional fees ran over budget, you can answer in five minutes with documents rather than in an afternoon with memory. Records made at the time, by the person who did the work, are worth far more than reconstructions made later.

Worked example two: the forecast

Now the more important number. Use the accepted fees of $14,550, including the queried block, because if the breakdown is reasonable you will pay it. The lawyer says the work is 60 percent complete.

Forecast at completion equals cost to date divided by percent complete: $14,550 divided by 0.60 equals $24,250. The cap is $18,000. The matter is heading $6,250 over the cap.

A second view gives the same message. The budgeted value of the work done so far is 60 percent of $18,000, which is $10,800. Actual accepted cost is $14,550. Divide budgeted value by actual cost: $10,800 divided by $14,550 is about 0.74. For every dollar spent, you are getting 74 cents of planned progress. Anything well below 1.0 deserves a conversation now.

Third, check the staffing. The blended rate, fees divided by hours, was $17,250 divided by 52.0 hours, about $332 an hour as billed. After corrections, valid hours are 52.0 minus 1.5 minus 4.0, which is 46.5 hours, and accepted fees are $14,550, giving about $313 an hour. Partner time is 10.5 of the 46.5 valid hours, about 23 percent. That is a reasonable mix for a negotiation; a much higher partner share would push the blended rate up, and a much lower one might mean junior lawyers are learning on your file.

What to do with the forecast

The cap is a contract term, so in principle the firm absorbs fees above $18,000 for this scope. In practice, a firm that sees itself losing money on a matter may slow down or staff it more thinly. The professional response is a short call: here is the review, here is the forecast, does the cap still hold, and is anything in the remaining work outside scope? Agree the answer in writing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying invoices without reading the time entries, so the overrun becomes visible only at the final bill, when your leverage is gone and the work is done. The control is a monthly review against the engagement letter, a written dispute note, and a forecast at completion every time.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner either pays everything to keep the relationship warm or disputes everything to look tough. Both damage the record. Pay what is clearly owed promptly, query what is unclear, reject only what the letter excludes, and say which clause you rely on.

Callback

In Week 12 we met work in progress and the idea that percent complete must be measured, not guessed. The same applies here. A professional's "60 percent complete" is an estimate, so ask what remains: which drafts, which meetings, which issues. Your forecast is only as good as that number.

Recap

Test every invoice for rate, duplicates, scope, vague entries and disbursements. Pay the clear amount, hold the queried amount, record the reasons, and forecast cost at completion against the cap while there is still time to act.

Next: LEX and Vera in the room, challenging your own lawyer's advice.
checklist: Keep the engagement letter beside every invoice you review
Check every rate against the letter
Search the time entries for duplicate dates and descriptions
Reject work outside scope unless you approved a scope change in writing
Query block-billed entries for a task breakdown rather than rejecting them
Check disbursements against the letter's terms
Forecast cost at completion as cost to date divided by percent complete
Send a written dispute note citing the clause for each item
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, an invoice is evidence, so test it. Keep the engagement letter beside it and run five checks: rate, duplicates, scope, vague entries and disbursements. In our hypothetical, a $17,250 fee subtotal contained a $750 rate error, a $750 duplicate call and $1,200 of excluded zoning research, leaving $14,550 accepted. A 6.5-hour block entry worth $1,950 was held for a breakdown, so $12,600 of fees was payable now, plus disbursements at cost. Then the more important number: at 60 percent complete, $14,550 divided by 0.6 forecasts $24,250 against an $18,000 cap. That is $6,250 over. Budgeted value of work done, $10,800, divided by actual cost gives 0.74: seventy-four cents of progress per dollar. Raise it now, agree in writing whether the cap holds, and record every query with the clause it relies on.
terms: Disbursements — out-of-pocket costs an adviser pays on your behalf and recharges, such as search fees and couriers.
Block billing — recording a large block of time with no breakdown of tasks, which makes the entry impossible to test.
Forecast at completion — the expected final cost of work, here estimated as cost to date divided by percent complete.

hostile.q: Your lender's monitor asks why legal fees on the acquisition are running 35 percent over the soft-cost budget line. What is your answer?
hostile.a: The firm's first invoice forecast $24,250 against an $18,000 cap. I reviewed it line by line, removed $2,700 of errors and excluded work, held a vague entry, and agreed in writing that the cap holds for the agreed scope. The excess you see is a separately approved zoning scope, funded from professional-fee contingency, with the approval attached.

title: The meeting where you challenge your own lawyer
summary: Challenging a professional's advice is a skill: you test the assumptions, the confidence and the downside without bullying the adviser into the answer you want. This scene shows the lines to use, the lines to avoid and how to leave with advice you can actually act on.
body:
You challenge advice to understand it, not to change it. The aim of the meeting is to leave knowing the assumption the answer rests on, how confident the adviser is, what it costs if they are wrong, and what would change their mind.

Recall

Q. At Enron, what was wrong with the outside review of the internal warning?

A. Public accounts describe its scope as limited, with the accounting largely not questioned. A review scoped not to look at the problem cannot clear the problem.

Q. When a vendor insists a transfer tax is "always the buyer's problem", what do you say?

A. That who bears the tax depends on the law and on the contract, and you will confirm both with your lawyer before agreeing the price.

Q. In a meeting where a broker quotes a land price, how do you test it without accusing anyone?

A. Ask what end value and return the price assumes, then do the residual yourself. Let the arithmetic do the challenging.

Why this matters

Owners fail with advisers in two opposite ways. Some accept every caveat and never act, which turns lawyers into a reason not to build. Others push until the adviser says what they want, which turns advice into a mirror. A developer who runs his own projects needs a third way: advice tested hard enough that you understand the risk, and then a decision that is yours.

The scene

This is a composite example. You are buying a site. Your lawyer has reviewed the title and emails: "There is a registered restrictive covenant from 1974 limiting the lands to residential use not exceeding two storeys. It may be unenforceable, but I cannot advise you to proceed on the basis that it is." Your plan is a four-storey rental building. The condition date is in nine days. You book a 30-minute call. Your project manager wants you to "push the lawyer to give us comfort". Vera is on the call to keep the record.

The lines to say

  1. "Help me understand the covenant before we talk about risk. Who benefits from it, and are they still around?" You start with facts, because covenant risk often turns on who can still enforce it.
  2. "What would have to be true for you to be comfortable that it does not stop four storeys?" This converts a no into a list of conditions you can test.
  3. "On a scale you are willing to put in writing, how confident are you that it is enforceable, and what is that view based on?" You want reasons, not adjectives.
  4. "If we proceed and you are wrong, what is the worst realistic outcome, and how fast would it arrive?" A covenant raised at rezoning is a delay; one raised after framing is a catastrophe. The timing changes the decision.
  5. "What are my options to reduce the risk before the condition date: a release from the benefiting owner, a court application, title insurance cover, a price adjustment or an extension?" You are asking for paths, not permission.
  6. "Please confirm in an email today the key assumption, your confidence and the three options, so I can decide by Friday." Vera will thank you for that sentence.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: "What would have to be true for the answer to be yes, and how would I find out before the condition date?"

The lines never to say

  • "Just tell me it is fine." You are asking the adviser to take your risk without the facts to do it, and a careful professional will refuse.
  • "Other lawyers would sign off on this." It invites a defensive answer and changes nothing.
  • "Can you leave that out of the letter?" Never ask a professional to soften the written record. It destroys the value of their advice and may compromise them.
  • "We have already committed to the lender." That is your problem, not a fact about the covenant, and it signals that you are about to make a decision under pressure.

The question behind the question

When the lawyer says "I cannot advise you to proceed", the question behind it is usually: "Do you understand that this is your decision and your risk, not mine?" Answer that directly: "Understood. I am not asking you to take the risk. I am asking you to help me size it." Most good advisers relax at that point and become far more useful, because you have removed the fear that you will blame them for a business decision.

The project manager's question behind the question is different: "Will this delay my schedule?" Answer it separately and later. Do not let schedule pressure enter the conversation with the lawyer.

When to stay silent

After you ask "what would have to be true", stop talking. The silence will feel long. Let the adviser think. The most useful sentence in the meeting often arrives after a pause of five or six seconds, when the professional moves from the rehearsed caution to their actual view. If you fill the silence with your own theory, you will get agreement instead of judgment.

Holding your state

Bad news on a condition date triggers the wish to fix it in the meeting. Before the call, write the decision you must make and the date you must make it on a card. During the call, keep your voice slower than feels natural and take notes instead of arguing. If you feel the urge to push, ask another question instead. After the call, take ten minutes before you speak to anyone else about it.

Worked examples: two endings

Ending one. You leave with a written email: the covenant appears to benefit a neighbouring parcel still owned by the original family; confidence it remains enforceable is described as material; the three options are a negotiated release, a court application with an uncertain timeline, or walking away. You use the condition date to approach the neighbour for a release, priced into the deal, and ask the vendor for a two-week extension. Decision made, risk sized, record kept.

Ending two. You push, the lawyer softens the language to "may not be a concern", and you waive the condition. Six months later the neighbour objects at rezoning. You have a softened opinion, no release and no leverage. Same covenant; different meeting.

Working with advisers: the monthly thread

Treat your advisers as a bench you build over years, not vendors you call in emergencies. Brief them on your strategy once a year, tell them when their advice turned out right, and tell them, plainly and without blame, when it did not. Professionals who understand your plans give sharper advice and flag risks you did not ask about.

Keep your own decision with you. An adviser frames risk; you choose. Write in your decision journal what the adviser said, what you decided and why. Review it after the outcome is known. Over time you will learn which advisers are cautious, which are accurate, and how to read each one.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer qualified where the land sits, on any covenant, title or land-use question.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is converting an adviser's caution into false comfort by pressure. The control is to ask for conditions, confidence and options in writing, and never to ask for softer words.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "I cannot advise you to proceed" as "no" and either abandons the deal or fires the lawyer. It usually means: the risk is real, here is its shape, the decision is yours.

Callback

In Week 6 we practised acknowledge, bridge, answer for hostile questions, and the line "I'll confirm by Friday". Today you are on the other side of that pattern. You ask the hard question, accept the adviser's acknowledgment of risk, and end by fixing a date for the written answer.

Recap

Challenge advice to understand it. Ask for the conditions behind a no, the confidence and its basis, the downside and its timing, and the options. Never ask for softer words. Stay silent after the key question, hold your state, and leave with the record in writing.

Next: Kema with the Week 25 quiz, the Red Pen and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Write the decision and its deadline on a card before the call
Start with facts before discussing risk
Ask what would have to be true for the answer to be yes
Ask for confidence with reasons, not adjectives
Ask for the worst realistic outcome and when it would arrive
Ask for options that reduce the risk before the deadline
Pause at least five seconds after the key question
End by fixing the date for written confirmation
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, you challenge advice to understand it, not to change it. When your lawyer says, I cannot advise you to proceed, they usually mean the risk is real and the decision is yours. So say: I am not asking you to take the risk, I am asking you to help me size it. Then ask what would have to be true for the answer to be yes, how confident they are and why, what the worst realistic outcome is and when it would arrive, and what options reduce the risk before the condition date. After the key question, stay silent for five seconds; the real view often comes after the pause. Never say, just tell me it is fine, and never ask them to soften the letter. Hold your state by writing the decision and the date on a card before the call. End by fixing a time for the written answer, then decide yourself, and record why.
terms: Restrictive covenant — a registered promise on title limiting how land may be used, which may bind later owners.
Condition date — the deadline in a purchase agreement by which a buyer must satisfy or waive a condition.
Qualified opinion — advice that comes with stated assumptions or reservations, which define how far you can rely on it.

hostile.q: Your own lawyer flagged a covenant limiting height, and you still want me to fund four storeys. Why?
hostile.a: Because we did not proceed on the lawyer's flag alone. We obtained a registered release from the benefiting owner, priced into the land deal, and the title insurer has confirmed cover for the covenant. I will give you the lawyer's written opinion on the release and the policy wording before you commit.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 25 review: using professionals well
summary: Six questions on engagement letters, instructions, privilege, fees and challenging advice, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical engagement letter, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week was about turning advisers from a cost into a control. If you can define the scope, instruct in writing, protect privilege, audit the invoice and challenge the advice, you will get far more from every professional you hire.

Recall

Q. From Day 3, why do fees move yield on cost so little while missed risks move it so much?

A. Fees are a small share of total cost, so an overrun changes the denominator slightly. A missed risk often removes income, and lost income is multiplied into lost value by the capitalisation rate.

Q. What were the four families of tax on the real estate tax map in Week 23?

A. Transfer taxes, value-added tax or goods and services tax, tax on gains, and recapture.

Q. From Week 17, what is the one-sentence logic of reverse engineering a deal?

A. Start from what the market will pay at the end and subtract everything else to reveal what the hidden numbers, like land price or required return, must have been.

Why this matters

Advisers sit at every gate of a development: buying land, raising money, building, selling and passing wealth on. The habits from this week apply to all of them, and they compound. An owner who instructs well gets better advice for the same fee on every project for the rest of his career.

The six questions

Question 1. What four things must an engagement letter settle?

Answer: Who the client is, what work is included, how the fee works, and what is excluded. The exclusions and the liability cap deserve the closest reading.

Question 2. What are the five parts of a written instruction?

Answer: The decision you must make, numbered questions, every material fact including the unhelpful ones, the documents, and the deadline with the reason for it.

Question 3. Name three features of privilege in common-law systems.

Answer: It belongs to the client, it generally protects advice rather than underlying facts, and it can be lost by sharing outside the protected relationship. The exact rules vary, so verify against the primary source.

Question 4. What did Enron teach about gatekeepers, and what is Rule 25?

Answer: That fees, narrow scope and closeness can erode independence until the check exists only on paper. Rule 25: I scope every adviser to look where the risk is, give them the whole file, and never let their fee depend on agreeing with me.

Question 5. An invoice is 60 percent complete with $14,550 of accepted fees against an $18,000 cap. What is the forecast at completion?

Answer: $14,550 divided by 0.60 equals $24,250, which is $6,250 over the cap. Raise it now and agree in writing whether the cap holds.

Question 6. Your lawyer says, "I cannot advise you to proceed." What is your first question?

Answer: "What would have to be true for the answer to be yes?" Then ask for confidence with reasons, the downside and its timing, and the options, all in writing.

Say that out loud now.

Say all six answers aloud, without looking, then check yourself against the text.

Recap of the week

Day 1: hire judgment, not paperwork, through a clear engagement letter, a written instruction and protected privilege. Day 2: Enron showed that gatekeepers fail when scope, fees and closeness erode independence. Day 3: fees move returns by basis points and missed risks by percentage points, so judge advice by expected loss avoided. Day 4: privilege covers advice not facts, conflicts need separate counsel, and liability caps need reading. Day 5: audit every invoice for rate, duplicates, scope, vague entries and disbursements, then forecast. Day 6: challenge advice to understand it, never to soften it.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical extract from an engagement letter for advice on buying a development site. Find the defects before reading on.

"We are pleased to act for you and your partners in connection with the acquisition. Our services will include such review of the transaction documents as we consider appropriate. Fees will be charged at our standard hourly rates, which may change from time to time without notice. Zoning, environmental and tax matters are excluded. Our total liability for any claim arising from this engagement is limited to the fees paid for the first month of work. Disbursements will be charged at cost plus an administrative fee. Please send any information you think is relevant."

The defects.

  1. "You and your partners": the client is unclear. If interests diverge, who does the lawyer act for? Name one client, and give partners their own counsel.
  2. "Such review as we consider appropriate": no defined scope. Replace with numbered questions tied to your decision.
  3. Rates that change "without notice": there is no budget or estimate. Require stated rates, an estimate, and notice before any change.
  4. Zoning excluded on a development site: the single biggest risk to value is outside scope. Either bring it in or engage a land-use adviser separately, in writing.
  5. Liability limited to the first month's fees: almost certainly far below the risk being advised on. Negotiate a sensible cap and confirm professional liability insurance.
  6. Disbursements "at cost plus an administrative fee": that is not at cost. Agree pure cost or a stated amount.
  7. "Information you think is relevant": it puts the burden of judging relevance on you. Your instruction should supply the full file, and the letter should say so.

Boardroom drill

Your task: explain to a new investor, in two minutes, how you manage professional advisers on a project. Speak it aloud and time it. Then compare it with this model answer.

Model answer: "Every adviser on our projects works under a written engagement letter that names the project company as the client, defines the scope around the real risks, and states rates and a budget. We instruct in writing with the decision we face, numbered questions, the full file and a deadline, and we ask advisers to restate the scope before they start. No adviser's fee depends on the answer they give. We review every invoice against the letter each month and forecast cost at completion, so overruns surface early. Legal advice stays within the solicitor-client relationship; we share conclusions with lenders and partners, not memos. And when advice is cautious, we test it for conditions, confidence and options rather than pushing for comfort. The result is that each dollar of fees buys a specific reduction in risk, and we can show you which."

Why the model answer works. It opens with the system, not with names of famous firms, because investors care how you control risk more than whom you hire. It uses concrete mechanisms an investor can check: letters, instructions, invoice reviews, a rule on fees. It addresses the investor's hidden worry, which is whether your advisers will protect you at their expense, by stating that the project company is the client and that partners take their own advice. And it closes with an offer of evidence. Score your own version on those four points: system first, checkable mechanisms, the hidden worry answered, and evidence offered.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is treating advisers as a compliance cost and not a control. The control is the system: letter, instruction, invoice review, and documented challenge.

The beginner's mistake

Signing the engagement letter the firm sends without editing it. It is a draft written to protect the firm. Read it as you would read a contract from a counterparty, because that is what it is.

Callback

In Week 2 you started a decision journal. Add one line to it for every significant piece of professional advice: what they said, what you decided, and what happened. In a year, that page will tell you more about each adviser than any reference check.

Recap

Define scope, instruct in writing, protect privilege, audit invoices and challenge advice without softening it. Rule 25 holds it together: independence is something you design.

head: The six questions
speak: Mr Shabazz, this week turned advisers from a cost into a control. Every adviser needs an engagement letter naming the client, the scope, the fee and the exclusions, and you read the exclusions and the liability cap first. Instruct in writing: the decision, numbered questions, every fact, the documents and the deadline. Privilege belongs to you, covers advice not facts, and is lost by careless sharing. Enron showed that gatekeepers fail when fees, narrow scope and closeness erode independence, which is Rule 25: scope advisers at the risk, give them the whole file, and never let their fee depend on agreeing with you. Fees move returns by basis points; missed risks move them by percentage points. Audit every invoice for rate, duplicates, scope, vague entries and disbursements, then forecast cost at completion. And when advice is cautious, ask what would have to be true for yes, never for softer words.
terms: Engagement letter — the contract with a professional that defines client, scope, fee and exclusions.
Privilege — protection for confidential legal advice that belongs to the client and can be waived by sharing.
Forecast at completion — the expected final cost of a matter, here cost to date divided by percent complete.

hostile.q: How do I know your advisers are working for the project and not just for you?
hostile.a: The engagement letters name the project company as the client, not me. Partners and investors are told in writing to take their own advice on anything where our interests can diverge, and fees never depend on outcomes. I will give you the list of advisers, their letters and their scopes, and you may speak to any of them about their independence.
